There is a lot of praise for the Metric system due to all of its units being a function of 1, 10 or 1/10th of another unit. This makes calculations involving distances, mass, volume, and temperature simple. However there are overlooked advantages to the Imperial System, mainly it's abundance of units. It is easier to communicate measurements when there are more units.

Starting with length, something small like half an inch; Most Americans have an intuitive understanding of how big half an inch is. Moving up, we get an inch, then two inches, all the way to six inches where we now have a choice to say half a foot. After twelve inches, we can now use feet and inches together or even fractions of yards, for example one foot six inches or one and a half feet or half a yard, or just eighteen inches. The imperial system allows lengths between a fraction of an inch to a small number of yards to be intuitively expressed with short interchangeable phrases.

Next, with weight, something like a quarter ounce; That's little heavier than a literal 25-cent quarter. Moving up we have half an ounce, an ounce, all the way to eight ounces, or half a pound, then a pound. If you are esoteric, at seven pounds you can say half a stone. With stones, you can describe your own weight with a number that is less than the number of fingers and toes you have. By combining ounces, pounds, and stones, and utilizing fractions, you never have to use a big number.

Lastly, with liquids, things get even better. Everyone knows how big a tea spoon is, and three tea spoons is half an ounce. Moving up to four ounces, we can say half a cup and at two cups, we can say half a quart, and finally at two quarts we can say half a gallon. There's so many units you almost never have to use a big number or a small fraction.

Hopefully I've illustrated why Imperial System is useful. The abundance of units gives lots of freedom to describe common things with short phrases that contain small numbers or basic fractions. This makes it an efficient system when speaking to somebody, which is import because at the end of the day, we are people.
